cards.explanation: The answer is that his soul refuses to be comforted. Asaph, the psalm's writer, doesn't pretend to be fine. In verse 2 he says, "my soul refused to be comforted." He's honest with God about how heavy the day is, and I think that honesty is worth noticing, friends.

The answer is that he groans and his spirit grows faint. Asaph, the psalm's writer, tells it like it is in verse 3: "I remembered You, O God, and I groaned; I mused and my spirit grew faint." Thinking of God didn't give him a quick lift in that moment. That's a man being real in a hard night.

The word is troubled. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says in verse 4, "I am too troubled to speak." I think he's so weighed down that the words just won't come. The verse also says his eyes won't close. That's a rough combo, friends.

The answer is the Lord rejecting His people. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says his spirit pondered at night, and in verse 7 it asks, "Will the Lord spurn us forever and never show His favor again?" Spurn means push away. I think it's brave to ask a question like that. He's asking, not deciding.

The answer is True. Verse 8 asks, "Is His loving devotion gone forever? Has His promise failed for all time?" Those are questions, not conclusions. Asaph lays them out honestly, and the psalm lets him.
The word is compassion. Verse 9 asks, "Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has His anger shut off His compassion?" Asaph is asking the question, not stating it as fact. Big difference, friends.

The answer is the right hand of the Most High. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says in verse 10, "I am grieved that the right hand of the Most High has changed." He says he's grieved. That's his own sorrow talking, and he says it straight. Then the next verse turns the whole psalm around.

The answer is the works of the LORD. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says in verse 11, "I will remember the works of the LORD; yes, I will remember Your wonders of old." See that turn? He goes from asking questions to choosing what to remember. I think that's the moment the whole psalm swings.

The answer is False. Asaph, the psalm's writer, says in verse 12, "I will reflect on all You have done and ponder Your mighty deeds." That's slow, careful thinking. He isn't skimming, he's settling in.

The question is, What god is so great as our God? Verse 13 says, "Your way, O God, is holy. What god is so great as our God?" Asaph asks it right after calling God's way holy. The question is a way of saying nobody compares. Nice and clear, friends.
The answer is the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Verse 15 says, "With power You redeemed Your people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph." Those are God's own people. Asaph names them by their family line.

The answer is that they swirl and even the depths shake. Verse 16 says, "The waters saw You, O God; the waters saw You and swirled; even the depths were shaken." Even the deepest parts got shaken. If I felt that, I'd hold onto my hat, and my gold base too.

The answer is False, and the text is loud about it. Verse 18 says, "Your thunder resounded in the whirlwind; the lightning lit up the world; the earth trembled and quaked." The earth is moving, no question.

The answer is True. Verse 19 says, "Your path led through the sea, Your way through the mighty waters, but Your footprints were not to be found." God's way goes through the mighty waters, and His footprints weren't found. That's a mystery I love.

The answer is like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron. Verse 20 says, "You led Your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron." Moses was Israel's leader, and Aaron was his brother (Exodus 4:14). A flock, friends, not a fancy parade. That's a gentle picture to end on.
